entries.title: lyx pause: stop every run at once, safely and on purpose
entries.brief: A hub-wide pause that interrupts every Claude session with Esc within seconds, unlike the step-boundary pauses, recorded as ordered so no failure or idle path fires
entries.body:
## Why

The operator suspends the laptop while runs are in flight.
A sleep can cut a network call or an agent turn midway (a weft push hung a batten run for 2.5 hours after a hibernate, #458), and after resume idle notices fire for time that was only sleep.

The existing `lyx batten pause` and `lyx loom pause` only set a request the machine consumes at its next producer boundary: they kill nothing, so an agent turn, a Webster batch or a review round runs on until it ends, which can be an hour.
That is not enough to make the hub safe to suspend.

## Proposal (operator, 2026-10-08)

- One hub-wide verb, named `lyx pause` (the operator's choice of name), that safely stops every lyx process within a short time.
- It gives running work a few seconds to finish cleanly, such as a bash command completing.
- It interrupts every running Claude Code instance by sending Esc.
- A pause is ordered and intentional: it must not trigger the paths for an unexpected stop, such as batten notices, the agents-idle or driver-dead conditions, review-round failures or crash recovery.
- The step-boundary pause is not good enough and goes: it is how Millhouse had to pause, and lyx now has the means to interrupt agents directly (shuttle's session state from hooks, the reed panes, shuttle's stop verb).

## Open design points

- Resuming: whether a matching verb resumes every paused run where it stood, and how each role takes up its interrupted turn (loom's `interrupt_policy` already distinguishes `reinvoke` from `handback`).
- Scope: whether the orch session is paused too, or only runs.
- Per-run use: whether `lyx pause <slug>` pauses one run the same way, now that the boundary pause goes.
- Relation to shuttle's stop verb from `shuttle-send`, which settles a run's record before removing its strand.

entries.title: reed: strands state their size; parallel agents share the window evenly
entries.brief: Replace the one collapse-all-but-the-newest rule with per-strand sizing: content-sized panes like the runs overview, and parallel agents that share space evenly
entries.body:
## Why

reed has one layout rule (`internal/reedengine/doc.go`, "The layout rule"): the strands stack in insertion order, every strand but the bottom-most takes `collapsed_rows` rows, and the bottom-most takes every remaining row.
It fits a run whose newest agent is the one that matters, and nothing else:

- `runs-overview` wants a small pane under the orch, sized to its content, with the orch above keeping the space; today the orch would collapse to `collapsed_rows` and the overview would grow.
- `multi-agent-producer` runs N agents in parallel, none more important than the others; each needs a large share of the window, and none may collapse.

## Proposal (operator, 2026-10-08)

- A strand states how it is sized instead of taking its size from its position.
- At least two kinds: a fixed or content-sized strand (the overview: as few rows as show all its lines), and a sharing strand that splits the remaining space evenly with the other sharing strands.
- The agents of one multi-agent step share the window evenly, side by side or stacked; which of the two is open.
- The collapsed stack of finished agents may stay as one kind among these, for strands kept only for reference.

## Columns (operator, 2026-10-08)

The layout rules need a broader revision: tmux under reed can show any arrangement, so stacking strands side by side in columns, rather than in rows, is tempting as the main rule.

## Open

- Side by side (columns) or stacked rows for parallel agents, or a rule by window width.
- Who sets a strand's kind: the spawning producer through its seat table (`multi-agent-producer`), or reed by role.
- How `runs-overview`'s content-sized pane learns its height as runs come and go, and whether reed re-applies the layout on each change.

entries.title: Compare fanned and solo review rounds from their usage records
entries.brief: A report over round usage records for the fan-on decision; a lost usage record shows in the facts
entries.body:
From review-lens-fan PR-Gate (2026-10-08): the Discussion and Plan fans ship off by default until round usage records show what they cost and find.

- A small report verb, or a batten run summary, compares the round usage records (`_lyx/reviews/*/round-N-usage`) of fanned and solo segments, so the operator gets the comparison without reading the records by hand.
- `excludedLenses` drops a whole focus file when the previous round's usage record is missing or unreadable and only logs a Warn, so a lost record silently widens a round back to the full fan; the run's facts should show it.

Operator (2026-10-10): the `standard` fan is turned on for Discussion-Review and Plan-Review in the prime loom config (`discussion_fan`, `plan_fan`) as a trial; after a few fanned runs land, an agent compares their round usage records against the solo rounds before this date.

## First fanned run: webster-replan-state Discussion (2026-10-10)

Read from the round-3 escalation, as lens tags in the review text (mentions, not unique findings):

| Round | generic | correctness | error-handling | test-gaps | Findings (B/M/L) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 6 | 2 | 4 | 2 | 3/6/5 |
| 2 | 6 | 4 | 5 | 3 | 1/9/9 |
| 3 | 6 | 3 | 1 | 8 | 1/9/6 |

Rounds 1 and 2 spent about 300k and 620k fresh tokens, of which the forks took 50% and 78%.
Blocking findings fell, but the total did not: each round found finer detail in the same decisions, much of round 3's from the `test-gaps` lens.
The loop hit its budget after round 3 and was granted a fourth round.

## Fan trial paused (operator, 2026-10-10)

The fan's design: the master reviewer reads most of what the round needs first, then forks, so each lens fork inherits that reading through the cache and needs little new reading, which keeps a fork cheap enough for a Sonnet medium reviewer.
In the first fanned run the forks' fresh tokens were 50-78% of a round (round 2: 485k over 5 forks, about 97k each) and their cache reads 12M, which suggests each fork read much on its own after the fork point.
The hub turned `discussion_fan` and `plan_fan` off, so Discussion and Plan review run the single `opus[medium]` reviewer again; pairs created before the change keep the fan.
The report compares the fanned rounds of `webster-replan-state` (and `cli-surface`, if its rounds fan) against solo rounds, and, before the fan goes back on, measures from the transcripts how much the master read before forking and what each fork read after it, so the fix targets the right side: the master's pre-read or the fork stencil's licence to read further.

## First analysis (2026-10-10, webster-replan-state Discussion rounds 1-4 and Plan round 1)

- Cause: the master forks after reading only the target, instructions and stencil (39-74k context), no code, then tells every fork to verify the Decisions' premises against the code. In Discussion round 1 the master read 19 code files (~35k) first, and its forks took 32 turns and 152k fresh; rounds 2-4 took 81-125 fork turns and 435-485k fresh.
- Inheritance works (each fork reads its 39-84k prefix from cache); cost scales with fork turns, about 3.5-4k fresh and ~100k cache read per turn. The correctness fork is the heaviest (33-63 turns). 32-46% of fork file reads duplicate another fork's.
- Fanned Discussion rounds cost 301-638k fresh against 86-121k for solo Opus rounds; Plan round 1 cost 901k fanned against 202-227k solo. About half of raw fork findings were duplicates across lenses; the fan raised more MEDIUM and LOW findings, not more BLOCKING ones.
- Responsible text: `clusterRulesBlock` in `internal/burlerengine/prompt.go`. "After exploring the target fully" never says to read the code the target cites, "Fetch only what your lens needs" sets no budget, and the master's own holistic review runs after the fork point, where no fork inherits it. The `standard` fan also points code lenses at design documents.
- Proposed fixes: the master reads all cited code before spawning but judges nothing there, since a review before the fork point would colour every fork, and each fork gets a tool-call cap (about 6); Discussion and Plan review use the existing `discussion` and `plan` fans (4 forks) instead of `standard`. Estimate: about 200-250k fresh per round, about 2x solo Opus instead of 5-6x.

entries.title: Spawn audit log: every process lyx starts is recorded and traceable
entries.brief: One recorded launch path and a hub-wide spawn log with owner, argv and resource use, plus a sampler and a summary verb, so a process storm can be traced after a crash
entries.body:
## Seen

On 2026-10-08 the operator's machine froze and needed a hard reset at about 20:12 CEST while four runs were in flight.
`sar` shows about 800 process starts per second between 19:50 and 20:00, about 500 more live processes by 20:10,
and the user slice at its 16 GiB `MemoryHigh` with swap full, so reclaim thrashed (8366 major faults/s, 768 MB/s reads).
Only about 15 claude sessions and 9 subagents started in that window, and nothing in lyx's logs says what else started the processes or which run, strand or command owned them.
The operator has seen an earlier storm of 100+ claude panes in reed, and could not trace that one either.

## Idea

Every process lyx starts goes through one recorded launch path that appends an audit line to a hub-wide spawn log:
time, pid, parent pid, the lyx command and trace id that started it, hub, run slug, strand name, executable and argv,
and on exit the duration, exit status, peak RSS and bytes read and written (from `rusage` and `/proc/<pid>/io`).
This covers tmux servers, sessions and panes, claude launches, git, and `go build`/`go test` in verify gates.
A sampler, such as the reed watchdog, also records per-strand process-tree counts and memory every few seconds,
so the state just before a freeze survives a reboot.
`lyx` gains a read verb that summarises the log by minute, run, strand and executable, so a storm can be traced to its source after the fact.

entries.title: Configurable file log level in logger.yaml
entries.brief: Trace files carry only high-level messages and logger.yaml sets no level; add a file log level so most of lyx can be traced on demand
entries.body:
## Seen

The trace files written for each lyx invocation hold only high-level messages, and `_lyx/config/logger.yaml` sets only retention (`trace_retention_count`, `trace_retention_days`).
The file log has no configurable level, so after the 2026-10-08 crash the traces could not show what lyx's subcommands did.
Activity-ranked pruning also left the per-minute invocation counts incomplete.

## Idea

`logger.yaml` gains a `level` key (error, warn, info, debug) for the file trace, independent of the `-v` console verbosity, with info as the default.
Every engine logs its decisions and external calls at info or debug, so raising the level makes most of what lyx does traceable without a rebuild.
The spawn audit stays always on, whatever the level, because it cannot be turned on after a crash.

entries.title: Lighter test suite: measured tiers, cheap tmux fixtures, no lingering children
entries.brief: Measure each tier, non-login shells and shared servers in tier 3, lyx built once, no background gc in fixtures (#472), a no-tmux scan for tiers 1-2
entries.body:
## Seen

On 2026-10-08 the integration tier dominated CPU during a Publish verify (`fabricengine.test` alone at 145%), and in the 53 hours before the crash tmux started 9,022 servers and 32,375 panes, nearly all from tier 3 tests, each pane a login shell that sources the operator's profile.
Tests in four packages link the `lyx` binary with cgo on their own, and `TestLoomResumeReconcilesTheHubConfigBeforeArming` flakes on `t.TempDir` cleanup because a git child, most likely a detached auto-gc, still writes into the fixture's object store (#472).

## Goal

- A measurement of every tier per package (time, CPU, peak memory, process count) with `cmd/testtiming`, on a quiet machine, before and after.
- Tier 3 panes run a non-login shell, and tests share one tmux server per package where isolation allows.
- `lyx` is built once per test run and reused across packages.
- Git fixture repositories are reused instead of built per test (operator, 2026-10-10): today most tests build their own repos and hubs through `gitkit` (about 1,400 calls, each spawning git) and tear them down again.
  A fixture shape is built once per package (or per test binary) and shared by every test that only reads it; a test that writes gets a cheap copy of the prepared fixture, not a fresh build.
  Tests that share one fixture must not see each other's writes, so Discussion decides per fixture which tests can share it as is and which need a copy.
  Measured 2026-10-10 on a loaded machine (four runs in flight): one git process costs about 1.3 ms to spawn, a minimal repo (init, config, one commit) about 9 ms, a `cp -a` of a ready repo about 2 ms; `go test -tags integration ./internal/fabricengine/` ran 631 tests in 26.5 s and spawned 50,045 git processes, about 80 per test.
- lyx's own code spawns far fewer git processes for lookups (operator, 2026-10-10).
  In the same `fabricengine` run, by subcommand: `rev-parse` 18,825 (38%), `worktree` 7,299, `commit` and `add` 6,227, `diff` 2,628, `clone` 2,279, `config` 2,092, `push` 1,620, the rest about 9,000.
  Most `rev-parse` calls are lookups (top level, HEAD, git dir, common dir) that can be read from `.git` in-process or cached for the process's life, in `internal/gitrepo`, `internal/gitexec` and `internal/lyxcwd`; that speeds up every `lyx` command, not only the tests.
  The run cannot split fixture calls from calls by the code under test, since both run in the test binary; the measurement goal above splits them first.
- Fixture repositories never auto-gc in the background, and every test waits for the git and lyx children it starts before its cleanup.
- A scan keeps tier 1 and tier 2 free of tmux.
- A static scan enforces `PATTERN-shuttle-stop`: `RemoveStrand` on a shuttle run's strand appears only in `shuttleengine` and the exceptions the entry names (`loomcli`'s removal of the loom driver's own strand, `orchcli`'s removal of the orch strand); the PR-Gate review of `shuttle-send` found the entry false against `orchcli` with nothing to catch it.

entries.title: Webster and round-gate bug sweep: replans, batch checks, fork sandbox, shell wait, test re-runs
entries.brief: Webster stays consistent across replans, its batch and fabric checks judge only what they should, implementer forks stay sandboxed, the shell wait leaves nothing running, and the round gate re-runs whole tests
entries.body:
## Goal

- A `lyx loom goto` back to Plan after Webster started leaves webster state consistent, so Webster never hard-fails on a plan fingerprint mismatch (#466).
- A Plan-Review round after the plan is implemented is not dispatched as a fix round that edits the plan webster recorded (#465).
- Rebaseline logs and names the silent overview-frame fallback when the baseline copy has no parseable Card Index.
- `commitsNamedBy` classifies every `head_sha` prefix candidate in one `git cat-file --batch-check` call.
- `verify-nested-module` (`crossModuleCommands` in `internal/planparser/verifymodule.go`) splits a verify chain at `||` and `|` as well.
- `lyx webster record-batch` applies create-not-done only to the cards of the batch it records, and its refusal names batch and card consistently (#484).
- An implementer fork cannot reach the real hub's fabric or remotes: its stencil states the sandbox-hub rule, lyx refuses `lyx fabric` writes and pushes to the hub's own remotes from an implementer strand, and `lyx fabric add --help` says it pushes (#494).
- The fabric-reference check allows read-only commands (`--help`, reads of fabric files, `git remote get-url`, `git ls-remote`), and `recover-batch` accepts pathless findings whose recorded commands are all read-only (#493).
- When Master's wait stops waiting on a background shell, lyx stops or records the shell, and the shell-wait rule is the same for transcript-reported and Stop-payload-reported shells (#496).
- The round gate's failing-test re-run (`publishFailureCommand` in `internal/loomshed/publishfailure.go`) runs the failing test's top-level test, never a subtest alone, since subtests may share state (#497).
- `TestLoomResumeReconcilesTheHubConfigBeforeArming` in `internal/loomcli` is deterministic (#492).
- A dead batch whose recovery left commits gets a second recovery without the orchestrator (#498; the turn-end classification half landed in 7462c1dc5).

The merged notes keep their own Seen sections below.

## From `goto-plan-stale-webster`

Imported from [issue #466](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/466).

## What happened

A loom run completed the Plan, Batchifier and Webster rows, then the Publish row went stuck and the run routed back (`goto`) to `Plan-Bouncer` several times.
The Plan loop edited the plan, and `Batchifier` re-ran and finished (`done`).
The next `Webster` step then halted the run as `failed` with anomaly `producer-hard-failure`:

```
webster: on-disk plan fingerprint does not match this run's recorded state: on-disk plan fingerprint e5774b7e... does not match this run's recorded fingerprint c14834a3...; the plan changed since state.json was created; way forward: 00-overview.md changed and is never rebaselined; restore it with "lyx webster restore-plan", or 1) lyx webster reset --to start; 2) re-step the Webster row
```

The run had 49 history entries when it halted.

## Why this is abnormal

The loom's own routing sent the run back through Plan after Webster had already created `state.json`, and then re-ran Webster against that stale state.
The recorded fingerprint can only match if the plan is untouched, so a legitimate Plan-loop edit made the next Webster step fail by construction.
Neither the `goto` to Plan nor the re-run `Batchifier` row reset or rebaselined webster state, so the failure was foreseeable from the recipe's own wiring rather than an operator or task-code error.
The error text offers manual recovery (`lyx webster restore-plan`, or `lyx webster reset --to start` and re-step), which a driver could have applied itself.

## What to do

When the loom routes back to a row upstream of Webster after Webster state exists, reset webster state (equivalent to `lyx webster reset --to start`) as part of that route, or have the Webster row detect a changed plan produced by an upstream re-run and rebaseline instead of failing.
Alternatively, make the recipe validate at the `goto` that a Plan re-entry invalidates downstream webster state.

Provenance: task slug `shuttle-send`; notes: `loom-halt.md`.

## From `plan-review-after-implemented`

Imported from [issue #465](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/465).

A Plan-Review round ran over a plan that was already approved and implemented by webster.
The review gained findings, but the fixer's only write surface was the plan, and webster could not accept a new card on this run's record.
`lyx webster rebaseline --card=[11,12]` was refused:

```
webster: the edited plan changes the cards of a batch this run already begun: 00-overview.md changed and this run recorded no overview frame, so the change cannot be confined to its Card Index; it carries the plan's integration verify and is never rebaselined; way forward: restore 00-overview.md, or 1) lyx webster reset --to start; 2) lyx webster run
```

The parent stopped all fixes mid-round, so every finding ended deferred.
The fixer also spent its orientation designing a new card that was then thrown away.

Why this is abnormal: the loom dispatches a review round whose fixes cannot land.
A frozen plan (webster already begun) makes the fix round unwinnable, and the only advertised way forward (`lyx webster reset --to start`) discards the implemented work.
The run records no overview frame, so a legitimate edit to the overview's Card Index cannot be confined and is refused outright.

What to do:
- Skip the fix-round dispatch, or tell the round prompt up front that the plan is frozen, when the run's webster record has begun a batch.
- Record an overview frame when webster begins a batch, so a Card Index change can be confined and rebaselined.

Provenance: task `shuttle-send`; notes `burler-plan-r1.md`, `webster-refusal-rebaseline.md`.

## From `overview-frame-fallback-log`

## Seen

The PR-Gate review of `webster-record-batch` (PR #473) found that `recordedOverviewFrame` in `internal/websterengine` returns an empty frame without logging when the stored baseline copy has no parseable Card Index, so the reason a rebaseline refuses on an old record is invisible.

## Idea

Log the fallback at Info with the baseline path, and name it in the rebaseline refusal.

## From `head-sha-batch-check`

## Seen

The PR-Gate review of `webster-record-batch` (PR #473) found that `commitsNamedBy` in `internal/websterengine/gitwrap.go` runs one `git cat-file -t` per object a short `head_sha` prefix names, and a 4-character prefix in a large repository can name many.

## Idea

Classify every candidate in one `git cat-file --batch-check` call.

## From `verify-module-or-pipe`

## Seen

The PR-Gate review of `plan-gate-checks` (PR #475) found that `crossModuleCommands` in `internal/planparser/verifymodule.go` splits a verify chain only at `&&`, `;` and newlines, so a `go` command after `||` or a pipe is read as part of the previous segment and its module is never checked.

## Idea

Split at `||` and `|` too.


## From issue #476

Imported from [issue #476](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/476).

## What happened

A plan card required one exact sentence to be added to the `PATTERN-shuttle-stop` line in `PATTERN.md`, with nothing else changed.
With that sentence the line is 409 characters, but `internal/pattern`'s `MaxEntryLineChars` caps an entry line at 320, and `TestOverview_RealFilePassesCheck` enforces the cap.
The plan was approved anyway, so the card could not be satisfied as written.

## Why this is abnormal

The implementer had to reword the whole line.
The reviewer, checking against the card's text, raised the reword as a finding (F1) and proposed a fix that fails the plan's own verify.
That produced extra Webster-Burler rounds on a defect that was fixed in the plan, not in the code.
The plan gate (Plan-Write, Plan-Bouncer) has no check that exercises a card's verbatim PATTERN text against the entry cap.

## What to do

Add a plan-gate check: when a card prescribes verbatim text for a `PATTERN.md` entry line, compute the resulting line length and reject the card if it exceeds `MaxEntryLineChars`.
Alternatively, tell Plan-Write in its instructions to check verbatim PATTERN text against the cap before approving the card.

Provenance: task `shuttle-send`; notes `burler-webster-r1.md`, `loom-halt.md`.

## From `record-batch-card-scope`

Imported from [issue #484](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/484).

`lyx webster record-batch 01` refused with a failed batch.
The refusal names batch `01-headcontains-bounded-walk` but blames card `3-proc-group-kill`: `create-not-done/3-proc-group-kill[blocking]: Create target "plan:internal/proc#ConfigureGroupKill" still does not resolve`.
The report was archived under `_lyx/webster/reports/` and the way forward given was `lyx webster recover-batch 01`.

Why this looks abnormal: the failing card's slug differs from the batch being recorded, so either the create-not-done check evaluates cards outside the batch being recorded, or the batch and card numbering are mixed up.
It is also unclear whether the "still does not resolve" check resolves the `plan:` symbol against the right tree (the worktree head versus the card's merged result), since the symbol was later made to resolve by a follow-up commit.
If the check is correct and the card simply had not created the symbol, this is a task defect and can be closed.

What to do: confirm that `record-batch` only applies create-not-done to cards of the batch being recorded, and that the refusal message names the batch and card consistently.

Provenance: task `git-robustness`; notes: `webster-refusal-record-batch.md`.

## From `fork-real-remotes`

### Seen

On 2026-10-10, `daemon-wakeups` batch 09's implementer fork ran `lyx fabric clone/add --help`, read the real hub's `_lyx/fabric/origin.json` and ran `git ls-remote` on the weft repo.
The card 14 fork's `lyx fabric add idle-a/b/c` pushed branches `idle-a`, `idle-b`, `idle-c` to `Knatte18/loomyard` and `idle-*-weft` to `Knatte18/loomyard-weft`.
Recovery refused the batch with `needs_fresh`; the parent reset it and recorded a sandbox rule as a decision.

### Idea

An implementer fork cannot reach the real hub's fabric or remotes: its stencil states the sandbox-hub rule (local bare repos as origins), and lyx refuses `lyx fabric` writes and pushes to the hub's own remotes from an implementer strand, the way the hub-wide config refuses writes from a task worktree.


### From issue #494

Imported from [issue #494](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/494).

An agent following a "scratch hub" procedure cloned the real weft remote and ran `lyx fabric add` three times.
Each call pushed its code and weft branches to the real origin, leaving stray branches on both the code and weft repositories.
Nothing in `lyx fabric add` output or `--help` made clear that it pushes, so the scratch hub was not isolated.

Suggested fix: document the push in `lyx fabric add --help`, and offer a flag or setting for a local-only add, or a way to point a scratch hub at a local bare remote.

Provenance: task `daemon-wakeups`; note `09-orch-held-injection-log.md`.

## From `webster-fabric-ref-check`

Imported from [issue #493](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/493).

`lyx webster record-batch 09` refused: an implementer fork's batch failed on four "fabric-reference violation" findings.
The flagged commands were read-only: `lyx fabric clone --help`, `lyx fabric add --help`, `lyx reed up --help`, `cat _lyx/fabric/origin.json`, `git -C loomyard-weft remote get-url origin` and `git ls-remote --heads`.
`lyx webster recover-batch 09` then refused with `needs_fresh`, because the findings name no path and recovery cannot check them.
The run halted `blocked` (escalation-to-human) at Webster until a binary-change re-step let it continue.

This is abnormal: the check treats any command mentioning the fabric as one that "can rewrite run state", including `--help` invocations and plain reads.
A fork that only reads help text or a config file cannot rewrite anything, so the batch fails and halts the run for no real violation.

Suggested fix: classify fabric-referencing commands, and allow `--help`, `cat`/`ls` of fabric files and read-only git queries (`remote get-url`, `ls-remote`).
Also make `recover-batch` able to accept findings that carry no path when every recorded command is read-only.

Provenance: task `daemon-wakeups`; notes `loom-halt.md`, `webster-refusal-record-batch.md`, `webster-refusal-recover-batch.md`, `driver-restep-2a77897a307a6691.md`.

## From `webster-background-shell-wait`

Imported from [issue #496](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/496).

A `webster-background-shell` note reported that Master's wait stopped waiting on a still-running background shell at a turn end.
The wait counts the turn end after `background_shell_wait_min` (10 minutes) for a shell only the transcript reports, and at once for one the Stop payload reports when Master's output files exist.
lyx did not stop the shell; it ended only because shuttle removes Master's strand when the run finishes.
The run's final outcome was `done`.

This is abnormal because a background shell can outlive the decision to stop waiting, and its output is lost without any record beyond the note.
Suggested fix: stop or explicitly report the shell when the wait gives up, or make the shell-wait rule consistent between transcript-reported and Stop-payload-reported shells.

Provenance: task `daemon-wakeups`; note `webster-background-shell.md`.

## From `subtest-rerun-shared-state`

Imported from [issue #497](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/497).

Seen (publish-recovery, 2026-10-10): the Webster-Burler round gate failed three times on `TestSmokeBootstrapLifecycle/died_driver_proceeds_to_the_success_envelope_and_logs_why` with "probe run lock: ... .lyx/shed/loom-smoke-task/run.lock: no such file or directory".
`publishFailureCommand` (`internal/loomshed/publishfailure.go:88`, from 7648e8b27) re-runs each failing test from `publish-failure.yaml` alone, with a `-run` filter anchored on the subtest (`^TestSmokeBootstrapLifecycle$/^died_driver_...$`).
That subtest depends on the scratch dir and run lock that the earlier subtests' `loom start` bootstraps create, so run alone it always fails, while the whole test and the full tmux tier pass.
The fixer looped on a failure its own fix could not touch, and the run needed an investigation and a parent decision.

Workaround: a parent decision that the failure is a gate artifact, then resume.

Expected: the re-run names the failing test's top-level test (the first `-run` segment), never a subtest alone, since subtests may share state.

## From `flaky-resume-reconcile-test`

Imported from [issue #492](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/492).

The webster integration-suite triage reported `internal/loomcli.TestLoomResumeReconcilesTheHubConfigBeforeArming` as flaky: it failed the first verify run and passed or vanished on rerun, with no change in between.

This is abnormal because a test that fails nondeterministically blocks verify gates, and the run in question halted blocked at Publish with "verify failed after merging parent branch" (anomaly `escalation-to-human`).
The halt note and the verify log on disk do not show whether this test caused that failure, so the link is unconfirmed.

What to do: reproduce with repeated runs of `lyx gate test --tags integration ./internal/loomcli`, find the ordering, timing or shared-state dependency in the test, and make it deterministic.

Provenance: task `bolt-and-store`; notes `webster-verify-triage.md`, `loom-halt.md`.


## From issue #498

Imported from [issue #498](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/498).

Seen (test-suite-weight, 2026-10-10): `lyx webster record-batch 01` refused on create-not-done, and `lyx webster recover-batch 01` spawned a recovery strand.
The strand committed a working fix (f4c8a9103), then ended its turn with "Batch gate is running; I'll write the report once it finishes".
`internal/websterengine/classify.go:43-45` classifies a turn end with no report as terminal `dead/asking`, and `awaitTerminal` (`recoverbatch.go`) stops the strand, so the report was never written.
Once dead, `record-batch` refuses, `begin-batch` reports the batch exhausted, and Master's stencil tells Master to stop on `dead`; the run blocked at Webster, and a `lyx loom goto --to Webster` plus resume blocked again on "Batch 01 is dead".

Workaround: the orchestrator ran `lyx webster recover-batch 01` again by hand; `RecoverSpawnOrAttach` spawns a fresh cold recovery strand when the prior record is terminal dead.

Expected: a recovery strand waiting on its own background gate is not dead at a turn end (wait for the shell, or its stencil forbids ending the turn before the report), and a dead batch whose recovery left commits gets a second recovery from Master or the Webster row without the orchestrator.

entries.title: Haiku 5.5 for the Bouncer judge: is its ruling simple enough
entries.brief: The driver already runs on Haiku 5.5; decide per Bouncer row whether the judge ruling is simple enough for Haiku, trial it, and switch only where it holds
entries.body:
## Seen

The operator benchmarked Haiku 5.5 on 2026-10-08 (`docs/benchmarks/haiku-5-5.md`): on one fully specified coding task it scored as well as Sonnet and Opus at medium, at a fraction of the cost, but took about twice as long and grew its context to 74–132k.
The driver steps one run through `lyx shed step` and answers its waits, and the judge rules on a fixed question per round; neither writes code or long prose.

## Driver switched (operator, 2026-10-08)

`driver` is `haiku[medium]` in `loom.yaml` from 2026-10-08, for runs started after that.
Compare the driver row of the token report per role, and the hub interventions, against the Sonnet runs before it.

## What the task decides: the judge (operator, 2026-10-10)

Switching the judge is one config key; the task's work is deciding whether it is sound.
The question is whether the judge's job is simple enough for Haiku 5.5: read what each Bouncer row's judge and seed passes receive and must rule on, and judge where a wrong verdict lets a defect through or sends good work back.

- Read the judge stencils and a sample of past verdicts from the usage and review records, and name the rows, if any, whose ruling needs more than Haiku holds.
- Trial the judge on Haiku on one run and compare against Sonnet runs: verdicts later overturned, extra review rounds, hub interventions and token cost.
- Switch only the rows where both the reading and the trial hold; the other roles stay as they are.

## Seen in use

- 2026-10-10, `bolt-and-store`: the Haiku 5.5 driver read its prompt, summarized its rules, and ended the turn asking "Tell me when to start", although the prompt says it runs autonomously with no operator to ask.
  The Haiku drivers of `multi-llm-producer` and `daemon-wakeups`, on the same prompt, started stepping at once; a message from the orch got it going.
  Fixed in 189fd59c8: the driver stencil now says the prompt is the go-ahead and a turn never ends on a question.

entries.title: Burler runs its round on MultiLLMProducer
entries.brief: The fixer becomes the chair and the reviewer advisor-1 in one seat table, replacing roundHalves and await-review
entries.body:
## Goal

Burler's review round runs on `MultiLLMProducer` instead of its own two-agent wiring (operator, 2026-10-08).

## Today

Burler's round has run two agents ad hoc since 572ab84e8: `roundHalves` in `internal/burlerengine/engine.go` starts the reviewer and the fixer, and the fixer waits on the review through `lyx burler await-review`.
The round wires six stencils (two orchestrator templates, three step files, a focus directive) plus per-segment rubrics through Go code spread over several packages.

## Wanted

- The fixer is the `chair` and the reviewer `advisor-1`, declared in one seat table.
- The ad hoc wiring (`roundHalves`, `await-review`) goes; the round's outcome, review files and Bouncer contract stay as they are.
- Fanned rounds (`discussion_fan`, `plan_fan`) keep working; whether a fan's lenses become advisor seats or stay forks of the reviewer is decided in Discussion.

entries.title: Plan-Write on MultiLLMProducer: advisors gather facts and check cards
entries.brief: Later: Plan-Write as the chair, with an advisor that maps callers, tests and verify commands per package, and possibly one that checks each card as it is written
entries.body:
## Seen

Plan gate rejects and Plan-Review rounds come mostly from facts the planner got wrong or missed: an uncovered caller, a verify line in the wrong module, a nested fixture module, a card over its test budget.
Plan is one document that must hang together, so two agents writing it at once would conflict.

## Idea

Plan-Write runs on `MultiLLMProducer` (task `multi-llm-producer`), the planner as the `chair`, with advisors doing work the chair would otherwise do itself:

1. A code-reading advisor maps, for each package the plan touches, its callers, tests, nested modules and verify commands, and answers the chair's questions from that map.
2. A card-checking advisor reads each card as the chair finishes it and checks its scope, `Edit:` list, verify lines and test budget, so the chair fixes it while its context is fresh rather than in a later review round.

A third shape, advisors writing the cards of their own batch from the chair's overview, is faster on large tasks but makes the cards hard to keep consistent; left out unless the first two fall short.

## When

Operator, 2026-10-08: later, after `discussion-multi-llm`.
Plan runs on `fable[high]` as a single agent from 2026-10-08; this is the next step if that does not reduce plan gate rejects and Plan-Review rounds.

entries.title: Batten idle notices count machine sleep as idle time
entries.brief: After a hibernate every run raises an idle notice for the whole sleep; the idle clock should skip time the machine was asleep
entries.body:
## Seen

The machine hibernated from 2026-10-08 22:17 to 2026-10-10 06:01 CEST with three runs in flight.
Minutes after waking, batten raised an idle notice for each run ("agents idle for 31h46m"), although every agent had resumed its turn and was working.
The orch has to check the system log for a sleep window before reading any idle notice (orch role, Investigating a stop).

## Idea

The idle clock measures time the machine was awake: it uses a clock that stops during suspend (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux rather than wall time), or drops a gap that matches a sleep window.
After a wake, a run is idle only once its agents have stayed quiet for the idle threshold of awake time.

entries.title: One owner for child-process lifetime in internal/proc
entries.brief: Fold lyx gate test's process-group, Pdeathsig and job-object setup into internal/proc beside ConfigureGroupKill
entries.body:
Two process-lifetime implementations exist once `gate-test-scope` and `git-robustness` both land: `internal/proc` `ConfigureGroupKill` (process group, group SIGKILL on cancel, shared by `verifyrun` and `gitexec`) and `lyx gate test`'s own child lifetime (process group, group kill on a caught signal, Linux `Pdeathsig`, Windows kill-on-close job object).
The orch kept them apart on 2026-10-10 so the two parallel branches would merge without conflict.

Idea: move the `lyx gate` child-lifetime setup into `internal/proc` beside `ConfigureGroupKill`, so one package owns child-process lifetime, and consider whether `verifyrun` and `gitexec` should gain the parent-death signal and job object as well.

The package also lacks a `doc.go`; its file headers carry the description (PR-Gate review of PR #483).

entries.title: CLI surface: a command index for the orch, one help form, intake keeps comments
entries.brief: lyx help index injected into the orch, a test-enforced form for Use/Short/Long including board payload keys, and intake that carries issue comments
entries.body:
## Goal

The orch knows every `lyx` command it may use without reading `--help` first, and every command's help reads the same way:

- `lyx help index` prints a generated one-line index of the command tree, and the orch watcher injects it into the orch's context (about 3k tokens; operator, 2026-10-10).
- Every command's `Use`, `Short` and `Long` follow one documented form, enforced by a test that walks the command tree.
  `[json-payload]` is fixed as part of that form, since it says too little: only `lyx board` takes a JSON payload, the payload form is the same for every board command, so it is stated once and each command's `Use` names its keys (operator, 2026-10-10).
  `set-deps` takes `id` like the other addressing verbs.
- `lyx board intake` carries issue comments onto the board.

The three parts below are the merged notes, each kept as written.

## Part 1: help index (#479)

Imported from [issue #479](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/479).

The orch needs an overview of every `lyx` command to choose among them; today it rediscovers them through `--help`, one module at a time.
A full help dump is too large to load, and the one-line descriptions Cobra already carries are almost small enough.

### Measured 2026-10-09

- Every command's `--help`, minus global flags, `-h` and the "Use … --help" hint: 141 commands, 4,100 lines, 159 KB, about 40k tokens.
  Most of it is design rationale and internal history rather than usage, such as `quarry --help` explaining when the `{"ok":false}` envelope appears.
- One line per command from Cobra's `Short`, nested by module: 140 lines, 12 KB, about 3k tokens.
- `lyx --help` runs in under 10 ms, so an in-process walk of the command tree costs nothing worth measuring.

### Proposal

- **`lyx help index`** walks the Cobra tree in memory and prints one line per command: its full path and its `Short`.
  It reads no files and caches nothing, so it always matches the running binary.
- **An internal annotation** on commands that only lyx itself or one role calls, kept out of the index injected into the orch, while `--help` still lists them.
  Examples: `lyx reed switch` (run by the Alt+Left/Alt+Right tmux bindings through `run-shell`), the `lyx webster` batch verbs, `lyx burler await-review`, `lyx fabric merge-stage`.
- **Consistent `Short` texts** that say when to use a command, not only what it is: today they mix capitalisation, and some say too little ("task-tracker board", "unified warp↔weft git-coordination").
- **Trimmed long help**: usage, flags and one example; design rationale belongs in the package's `doc.go`.

### Who gets the index

Only the orch, and the operator's own sessions.
A spawned role gets the exact commands it runs from its stencil and nothing more: the driver runs `lyx shed step`, Merriam the `lyx webster` batch verbs, the planner `lyx quarry`.
More would only give a role commands it should not run.

- **The orch:** the watcher injects the index at `lyx orch start`, at `--adopt` and after every cycle, since a compaction drops what was loaded.
  The prompt says the index is complete and `lyx <command> --help` gives the details, so the orch never needs to call `lyx help index` itself.
  Same mechanism as the skill loading in `lyx-skills-and-stencils`.
- **The operator's sessions:** a skill with a short workflow section and `` !`lyx help index` `` in its `SKILL.md`, so Claude Code runs the command once when the skill loads and the content is always current.

### Why a CLI index, not an MCP server

An MCP server configured for the project loads into every Claude session started there, every spawned Burler, Webster and driver session included, so every role pays for tools it must not use.
With the CLI, only the orch pays for the index, and the CLI is already built, tested, and the same for an agent and a person at a terminal.


### Issue comment, 2026-10-09

Measured a variant with each command's signature on its line: the first `Use` line (minus `[flags]`), then the flag names without descriptions, then `Short`.

```
- `lyx batten goto [<run-id>] --to <producer>` `--to`: move a halted lifecycle onto a named row, paused, with a fresh segment budget
- `lyx board upsert [json-payload]` `--body-file`: Create or update a single task
```

140 lines, 14 KB, about 3.5k tokens: about 500 tokens more than the `Short`-only index, and the orch can call most simple commands without a `--help` first.
Flag descriptions would add another 14 KB and are not worth it.
Proposal: `lyx help index` prints this form.

The walk also showed that `Use` and `Short` follow no common form (flags inside `Use` on some commands, mixed argument spellings, `[json-payload]` without keys, mixed capitalisation), which makes the index uneven; filed separately as #480.



### Issue comment, 2026-10-09

### Marking who a command is for, at the Cobra level

"Internal" covers two different things: a command only lyx's own Go code or a key binding runs, and a command one spawned role runs because its stencil names it.
Neither belongs in the index injected into the orch's prompt.
Both stay visible in `lyx --help` (operator decision, 2026-10-09): the annotation decides what the orch is handed, never what help shows.

Proposal:

- **An `audience` annotation on every command**, in Cobra's `Annotations` map (lyx already uses it, such as `clihelp.SkipStencilSeedAnnotation`), with a closed set of values:
  - `operator`: the orch and the operator's own sessions.
  - `role`: a spawned role that gets the command from its stencil.
  - `internal`: only lyx's Go code or a key binding.
- **A test walks the command tree** and fails on a command with no `audience` or a value outside the set, so a new command cannot skip the decision.
- **`lyx help index` prints `operator` commands by default**; `--audience role` exists for inspection, though a stencil should name its role's few commands directly.

### Shorter index lines

Each line names only its own command word and the rest of its signature, since `lyx` and the parent path are implied by the nesting, and lists only flags its signature does not already spell:

```
- `batten`: drive one task worktree's whole lifecycle as a single Shed run
  - `goto [<run-id>] --to <producer>`: move a halted lifecycle onto a named row, paused, with a fresh segment budget
  - `run [<run-id>]` `--child-driver --driver --window`: start or resume a task worktree's whole lifecycle run to its next halt
```

That saves 11–12% (14.2 KB to 12.6 KB with signatures).
`Short` texts are not to be shortened; some are too short to say when a command applies (#480).

### A first classification

From the command index and who calls each command, as a starting point to review once when the annotation lands; about 45 of 140 commands are `role` or `internal`:

| Module | Commands | Called by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reed | `switch`, `watchdog`, `add`, `resume` | the Alt+arrow bindings, the watchdog daemon, shuttle and orch code |
| shuttle | `run`, `send`, `interrupt`, `state` | the Go code that spawns agents |
| burler | `run`, `await-review`, `validate-review` | the round's Shed row and the fixer |
| webster | `begin-batch`, `await-batch`, `record-batch`, `recover-batch`, `run`, `rebaseline`, `restore-plan`, `accept-audit`, `validate`, `verify` | Merriam and the recovery session |
| loom | `step`, `run`, `commit-records`, `validate-plan`, `validate-discussion`, `validate-description`, `lint-comments`, `decision add`, `review delivered`, `review notify` | the driver and the writers |
| shed | `seed`, `step`, `run` | batten and the drivers |
| fabric | `merge-in`, `merge-stage`, `commit` | landing's Go code |
| quarry | `glyphs`, `resolve`, `toc`, `expand` | the planner |

Borderline: `webster status`, `webster reset` and `shuttle state` may serve the orch when it diagnoses a stuck run.





## Part 2: a common form for Use, Short and Long (#480)

Imported from [issue #480](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/480).

The `Use` and `Short` texts of lyx's Cobra commands follow no common form, so a generated command index (#479) and every `--help` an agent reads are uneven.
Found 2026-10-09 by walking every command's `--help` (140 commands).

### `Use` lines

- **Flags inside `Use` on some commands, not on others.** 13 commands spell flags into `Use`, so a help page lists them twice (in `Usage:` and `Flags:`), while every other command leaves them to `Flags:`.
  Examples: `lyx fabric clone [--shortname <shortname>] [--reset] [--subpath <rel>] [--force-bootstrap] [--into <dir>] <weft-url> [<warp-url>]`, `lyx fabric cleanup [--apply] [--force] [--remote]`, `lyx fabric remove [--force] [--remote] <slug>`, `lyx loom review approve [slug] [--review <file>]`, `lyx shed seed <run-id> --recipe <name>`.
  A required flag (`goto --to <producer>`, `shed seed --recipe <name>`) is a fair exception; an optional one is not.
- **Argument spelling differs:** `lyx batten goto [<run-id>]` and `lyx shed goto [<run-id>]`, but `lyx loom goto [run-id]` and `lyx loom review approve [slug]`.
- **`[json-payload]` names no keys.** The 10 board commands that take a JSON payload say only `[json-payload]`; the keys are in the long help, so an agent always needs `--help` before a first call.
  A short key list in `Use` or in the first line of the long help, such as `upsert '{"slug", "title"?, "brief"?, …}'`, would be enough for most calls.

### `Short` lines

- **Capitalisation is mixed:** 36 start with a capital letter (all 20 `board` commands, `stencil`, `quarry`, `ide`) and 104 with a lower-case one.
- **Some say what a module is, not when to use it:** `lyx board`: "task-tracker board"; `lyx fabric`: "unified warp↔weft git-coordination".

### Expected

One documented form for `Use` and `Short`, enforced by a test that walks the command tree, as `PATTERN.md`'s other CLI rules are:

- `Use` carries positional arguments in one spelling (`<arg>` required, `[<arg>]` optional) and required flags only.
- `Short` starts in lower case, has no final period, and says what the command does in terms of when to reach for it.


### Issue comment, 2026-10-09

### `[json-payload]`: name the shapes once, reference them per command

Only `lyx board` takes a JSON payload, in 10 commands.
The form is always one JSON object with unknown keys rejected, and the keys fall into a few shapes that recur across commands:

| Shape | Keys | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<addr>` | `slug` or `id` | `get`, `remove`, `promote`, `set-status`, and `merge`'s `set_status` |
| `<task>` | `slug`, plus optional `title`, `brief`, `body`, `depends_on`, `isolated`, `status`, `kind`, `labels`, `recipe`, `short_name` | `upsert`, each element of `upsert-batch`, `merge`'s `upsert` |

Proposal: define each shape once, in the `lyx board` group's help, and have each command's `Use` reference it instead of saying `[json-payload]`:

```
board: payload shapes: <addr> = {slug|id}; <task> = {slug, title?, brief?, body?, depends_on?, kind?, labels?, …}
  get <addr>
  remove <addr>
  promote <addr>
  set-status <addr>+{status}
  set-deps {slug, depends_on}
  upsert <task>
  upsert-batch {tasks: [<task>]}
  merge {remove_slugs?, upsert: <task>, set_status?: <addr>+{status}}
  intake close {issue, reason, completed?}
  intake import {issue, slug|into, title?, brief?, labels?}
```

The shapes are then stated in one place, the command index (#479) carries them for the cost of one line, and an agent can call most board commands without reading `--help` first.
A test can hold the shapes and the payload parsers together, so a key added to one cannot be missing from the other.

### `set-deps` takes no `id`

`get`, `remove`, `promote` and `set-status` address an entry by `slug` or `id`; `set-deps` takes `slug` only.
It should take `<addr>` like the others.



### Issue comment, 2026-10-09

### Long help: too long at the top

Every command's `--help` together is 159 KB, about 40k tokens.
The median page is about 740 bytes, which is fine; the problem is the top, where about ten pages run 2.5–5.4 KB each:

| Page | Bytes |
| --- | --- |
| `lyx loom` | 5,419 |
| `lyx webster` | 5,088 |
| `lyx fabric clone` | 4,973 |
| `lyx loom start` / `lyx start` | 4,385 / 4,380 |
| `lyx webster reset` | 4,157 |
| `lyx fabric cleanup` | 3,936 |
| `lyx webster validate` | 2,866 |
| `lyx loom resume` | 2,782 |
| `lyx fabric remove` | 2,740 |

Measured 2026-10-09 by walking every command's `--help`, without global flags, `-h` and the "Use … --help" hint.

Three patterns recur:

- **A group page restates its subcommands in prose.** `lyx loom --help` describes all its subcommands in one long paragraph, and Cobra then lists them again under "Available Commands"; the list alone is enough.
- **Implementation detail.** `start` "seeds the status file, commits the seed, and spawns/attaches the detached driver session"; `fabric clone` explains that the binding is "a plain single-line record, .lyx-warp, kept at the board root".
  That belongs in the package's `doc.go`.
- **Edge cases and refusals stated up front.** `fabric clone` spends several paragraphs on when `--reset` and `--subpath` are refused.
  The error message at the moment of refusal, naming the remedy, serves better.

Proposed norm for `Long`: what the command does, when to use it, what its arguments and flags mean, and one or two examples.
Everything else moves to `doc.go` or to the error messages.
Under that norm the largest pages would likely shrink to about a third, which also makes `lyx <command> --help | grep …`, the orch's usual lookup, cheaper and less noisy.





## Part 3: intake carries issue comments

`lyx board intake import` writes only the issue title and body (`issueContent` in `internal/boardengine/intake.go`); `selfreportengine` never fetches comments, so every comment on an issue is lost at import.
The operator treats a comment as part of its issue: #479 and #480 carried as much in comments as in their bodies and were completed by hand on 2026-10-10.

### Expected

- `import`, for a new note and for `into`, appends each comment after the body under a `## Issue comment, <date>` heading, oldest first.
- `intake list` shows the comment count, so an orch sees that an issue has comments before it decides how to import it.
- The pointer comment lyx itself posts on import is never carried back in.

entries.title: shuttle raises a hold notice at the skill-load turn end, before the start prompt is sent
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #485](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/485).

On 2026-10-10 at about 07:07 the orch got a hold notice for `ly:bolt-and-store:discussion`: "ended a turn without its output files and is held … Its last message: «ok scribe:prose, scribe:conversation»".
That last message is the reply to shuttle's own skill-load prompt.
The pane shows the start prompt ("Read …/prompt.md in full first …") typed right after it, and the agent working on its task within seconds.
So the hold check judged the skill-load turn end as a task turn end that lacked its outputs, and the orch was woken for nothing.

## Expected

- The turn end that answers the skill-load prompt (and any other turn shuttle itself injected before the start prompt) never counts as a task turn end for the hold check.
- A hold notice is raised only after the start prompt was sent and a later turn ends without the outputs.

entries.title: Driver steps in only on trouble: Go loops the steps, context under 100k
entries.brief: Go runs the shed steps and wakes the driver only at a stop, so a Haiku driver stays under 100k; the driver can still stop a run at a point the orch names
entries.body:
## Goal

The driver steps in only when something goes wrong, and its context stays under 100k tokens for a whole run, since Haiku 5.5 is cheap only below that.
Build idea 1 below: Go runs the steps in a loop and wakes the driver only at a stop (error, interrupt, blocked, awaiting gate, run end).
Ideas 2 to 6 come along where they still apply once the loop is in Go; idea 7 is optional.

`lyx shed step` says too much on success and too little on failure: a successful step prints its envelope plus stderr slog noise the driver must read, while a failed one prints too little, so the stencil has the driver read every step's trace in case a later failure needs it before retention sweeps it.
Turn that around:
- A successful step answers in one short line, and the driver reads almost nothing before the next step.
- A failed or stopped step answers at length: what went wrong, the trace lines that matter, and the paths to read further, so the driver can act on the answer itself and opens the trace only to dig deeper.
- Retention never sweeps the trace of a step that failed or stopped before the driver has handled it, so the driver never reads a trace pre-emptively, and the stencil drops "After every step, read its `trace_file` right away".

The heavy work at a failure goes to a one-shot fork of the driver: reading traces, reports and logs, and writing the distilled report it sends to the parent.
The fork returns only its conclusion and the action to take, so the driver's own context stays clean across many stops.
With the Go loop the driver's context stays small, so a fork that inherits it is cheap and stays under 100k too.

The orch must still be able to tell the driver, in plain words, to stop the run at a chosen point, for example "stop after Batchifier, before Webster", and the driver must hit that point itself.
`lyx loom pause` is not the route: it is too restrictive.
So a stop condition, such as a producer to stop before or after, is recorded in the run's own state by a command, and the Go loop reads it between steps, stopping there before the next producer starts and waking the driver.
Setting it never restarts the loop or interrupts a running producer: the producer in progress always finishes.
A message to the driver still reaches it promptly while the loop runs, and the driver turns such a request into that command, using the producer names the step envelope and the recipe give it.

The Go loop also watches its own steps: a step that never returns is noticed and stops the loop as a failure that wakes the driver, so the hub never has to read panes to find a hung `lyx shed step` (from `verify-watchdog`, #420).

A failed step never parks silently (from `driver-silent-park`, #488).
In `bolt-and-store` (2026-10-10) a Webster-Bouncer step returned `ok:false` with no `kind` and no trace, because a hub config file (`_board/_lyx/config/landing.yaml`) a later deploy added was missing; the driver wrote a drive report, parked with `commit-records --park` and told the parent nothing, while the run stayed `running`.
The hub heard of it only through batten's quiet notice, and `lyx loom resume` answered "the run is already running".
So a step failure without a `kind` is a stop that reaches the parent, as a halted run or a driver escalation, and the missing-config refusal gets its row in the refusal spec.

## Seen

A study of 19 driver sessions (2026-10-10) found that every finished run's driver passed 100k tokens of context, peaking at 112k to 190k.
They cross around API call 80 to 115, mid-run, at Plan-Review, Webster, Webster-Review or Batchifier.
Haiku 5.5 is cheap only below 100k, and the Haiku drivers grow faster per step (4.0k to 4.7k) than Sonnet (2.2k to 3.6k), since they `cat` whole trace files.
There is no compaction, so the peak is the last turn.

The growth is a fixed cost per step, not one big item: each `lyx shed step` cycle takes four API turns and adds 2.2k to 4.6k tokens, over 35 to 47 steps per run.
Of 1.98M tokens of growth across the sample:

| source | share |
|---|---|
| assistant output, thinking included | 24% |
| Read of the step's background output (envelope plus stderr) | 19% |
| trace reads after every step | 15% |
| task-completion notice per step | 12% |
| harness attachments | 9% |
| prompt.md and skill body | 7% |
| background-launch result | 4% |
| `lyx shed status` | 4% |
| Reads of the files a step's `output` names, mostly `decision-record.md` at 13 to 25KB | 2.5% |

The start is about 20.5k (tool schemas about 6k, the skill listing about 5 to 6k, system prompt and CLAUDE.md about 4k), then about 30k after the `scribe:prose` body and the 18.9KB `prompt.md`.

Noise rides along in step stderr:
- the plan gate's informational findings as one WARN line of up to 25KB (`internal/loomshed/gates.go:199`), 172KB across the sample;
- `stencilstore: board copy has drifted` up to 58 times per run (`internal/stencilstore/reconcile.go:236-240`), 106KB;
- full Go SIGQUIT goroutine dumps of about 20KB when a step is killed, 76KB.

Report writing (drive reports, SendMessage, friction) is about 3k tokens per run, so having the driver fork itself for reports would not help: each fork does a full cache read of the parent's context and starts above 100k whenever the parent does.

## Idea

Ranked by whether it keeps a whole run under 100k:

1. Go loops the steps and wakes the driver only at a stop, for example `lyx shed step --until-stop` in `internal/shedverbs/step.go`, keeping each step's trace for the driver.
   It saves 80 to 130k per run, with peaks of about 35 to 50k, and is the only single change that reliably keeps a Haiku driver under 100k.
2. The driver reads a step's trace only on an error, interrupt or stop, not after every step (`contracts/stencils/shed/shed-template-driver.md`); Go keeps the trace of a failed step.
   It saves 25 to 45k per run.
3. Keep slog WARN lines and stack dumps out of the step's stdout and stderr and send them to the trace: a count instead of the full plan gate findings, the drift warning once or at debug, the SIGQUIT traceback to the trace file.
   It saves about 7k per run, 20k on a run with many gate findings.
4. Drop "reading the artifact `output` names when it is non-empty" from the stencil: 0 to 10k per run.
5. A slimmer start: drop `scribe:prose` from `driverSkills` in `internal/loomcli/driverspec.go`, keep the skill listing and unused tools (Agent, ListAgents) out of the driver session, and move the stencil's rare branches to a file read on demand: 10 to 13k per run.
6. A compact envelope from `lyx shed step` and `lyx shed status`, without `remaining`, empty fields and repeated absolute paths: 6 to 10k per run.
7. Lower effort or thinking for Sonnet drivers: about 10k.

Changes 2 to 6 without 1 bring a 45-step run to about 90 to 95k, borderline.


## From issue #491

Imported from [issue #491](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/491).

Seen (daemon-wakeups and bolt-and-store, 2026-10-10): after `lyx loom approve` at PR-Gate, batten read the approval, resumed the child and woke the parked driver.
Each driver then checked the PR on GitHub (`gh pr view`), saw it OPEN with no review decision and history unchanged, concluded nothing was decided, wrote a stop report, parked again and asked the operator to approve.
`lyx loom approve` writes a local record (`<pair>-weft/.lyx/loom/approval.json`) and never posts a GitHub review, so a driver judging by GitHub can never see an approval.
Batten counts the decision as acted on and does not try again, so both runs hung at PR-Gate.

Workaround: the orchestrator messaged each driver that the PR is approved and to step with `lyx shed step`.

Expected: a woken driver at an awaiting PR-Gate steps the run (or reads the decision through a `lyx` verb), never judges a decision by the GitHub PR state; the driver stencil says so.

entries.title: PATTERN overview breaks its cap only after merging main
