entries.title: Build-tagged member declared once per tag set resolves ambiguous, so its plan Create can never pass record-batch
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #500](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/500).

Seen (test-suite-weight, 2026-10-10): plan card 10 declares `plan:internal/testkit/tmuxkit#tmuxAllowed` as a Create, implemented the idiomatic Go way: `const tmuxAllowed = true` in `allow_tmux.go` (`//go:build tmux || llm`) and `const tmuxAllowed = false` in `allow_none.go` (`//go:build !tmux && !llm`).
`lyx quarry resolve internal/testkit/tmuxkit#tmuxAllowed` returns `status: ambiguous` with both files as candidates, because quarry ignores build constraints, and record-batch's DoneChecks accept only `found` or `multipart`, so the batch fails `create-not-done` however it is implemented.
The recovery strand stopped to ask, and nobody in the run may edit `_lyx/plan` to drop the glyph.

Workaround: a parent ruling to restructure the code into one `var` plus an `init()` in the tagged file, listed as deviations.

Expected: a member declared once per mutually exclusive build-constraint set resolves (quarry honours build constraints, or DoneChecks accept an ambiguous answer whose candidates all sit in files with disjoint build tags); and the plan validator flags such a glyph at Plan time rather than at record-batch.


## From issue #507

Imported from [issue #507](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/507).

A Go symbol with one body per GOOS (for example `StartTime` in `internal/proc`, or `runChild` and `terminatingSignals` in `internal/gatecli`) is answered `ambiguous` by `lyx quarry resolve`.
A plan can therefore neither `Edit` nor `Delete` such a symbol by glyph.
The only spelling the gate accepts is the file path, so retiring the symbol means deleting whole files.

The gate then refused `create-already-exists` for a `plan:` handle whose name matched a symbol those deleted files declared, because the resolve pass reads the tree before any card runs.
The plan had to rename the replacement symbols and edit their callers, a rename the design never asked for.

This is abnormal: the same card both deletes every declaration of the name and creates it again, and the plan is coherent.

What to do, either of:
- let a `Create` handle reuse a name whose every declaration the same card deletes;
- make `lyx quarry resolve` treat per-GOOS bodies of one symbol as a single declaration, so glyph `Edit` and `Delete` work.

Provenance: task `driver-context`; note `Plan-Write.md`.

entries.title: Bounce budget blocks a review segment after its round was approved, before the Bouncer verdict
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #503](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/503).

Seen (publish-recovery, 2026-10-10): Webster-Review's round 3 review was APPROVED (one LOW finding) and its fixer finished with a green verify gate, but the run blocked with "bounce budget exhausted for Webster-Burler" before the Bouncer wrote `round-3-bouncer-verdict.md`.
`lyx loom circling accept` refused, since the run was blocked rather than awaiting, so the orchestrator needed an investigation fork, then `lyx shed goto publish-recovery --to Webster-Burler` and `lyx loom resume`, which spent another review round on approved work.

Workaround: goto Webster-Burler plus resume.

Expected: the bounce budget is checked before a round starts, not after an approved round ends, so a round whose review approved always reaches its Bouncer verdict and the run moves on.

entries.title: Darn recipe: one producer, then the usual PR; shared Publish, Finalize and teardown fixes
entries.brief: The darn recipe: a simplified run for small changes (one producer, verify retries to a budget, PR-Gate as usual), plus per-attempt verify logs, Finalize ignoring the parent weft batten records, teardown clearing abandoned claims, and Reflect reading the parent weft
entries.body:
## Seen

Small cosmetic or narrow changes, such as `board-priority-headings`, are too small for a full loom run (Discussion, Plan, Webster, review rounds), so today they go to a hand-briefed agent in the prime instead.
That path skips the pair, the preflight, the verify gate, the PR and PR-Gate, and the orch has to brief, watch and land each one by hand.

## Idea

A second task recipe, `darn`, for quick tasks, run through batten and shed like a loom run but with a strongly simplified loom inside:

- the same outer lifecycle: batten creates the pair, preflight runs, and teardown removes the pair after landing;
- one LLM producer that does the whole change in a single session: reads the board entry, edits, runs the tests and commits;
- the usual Publish: verify gate, PR, the orch's PR-Gate with a reviewer fork, then Finalize.

No Discussion, no Plan, no Webster, no Burler rounds.
## Operator decisions (2026-10-10)

- The operator picks the recipe when the task is created, through the board entry's existing `recipe` field; no size guard.
- A failed verify sends the run back to the same producer to fix it, up to a configured budget of attempts; past the budget the run escalates to the parent.
- The recipe is named `darn` (mending a small hole in the fabric); it is never called "loom".

## Prime agents block runs (2026-10-10)

A hand-briefed agent editing in the prime leaves it dirty, and `lyx batten run` then stops at Worktree-Create ("source worktree has uncommitted changes") until the agent pushes, as `cli-surface` did while the seats N=0 prompt fix (abe2aa50e) was in progress.
The quick recipe runs such fixes in their own pair, so the prime stays clean; the operator wants the orch's prime-agent fixes to move to it over time.

## Folded in: shared Publish, Finalize and teardown fixes

The quick recipe reuses loom's Publish and Finalize and batten's teardown, so these fixes land with it.

### Verify log per attempt (#502, from `verify-log-overwritten`)

Seen (publish-recovery, 2026-10-10): the Publish verify failed once (exit 1, the #497 subtest re-run), and a later verify run overwrote `.lyx/verify/verify.log`, so Friction-Reflect could not read the original failure and reflected on the later, passing log.
Expected: the verify log is kept per attempt (for example `verify-<attempt>.log`, or appended with an attempt header), so a later run never erases the evidence of an earlier failure.
The quick recipe's verify-retry loop needs this, since its producer fixes the failure the log records.

### Finalize ignores the parent weft's batten records (#501, from `finalize-weft-batten-dirty`)

Seen (publish-recovery, 2026-10-10): after `lyx loom approve`, Finalize stopped blocked with "fabricengine: merge preconditions failed: worktree dirty".
The task pair and its weft were clean; the dirty tree was the prime's weft, holding uncommitted batten records (`_lyx/shed/<slug>/status.json`) of sibling runs.
Batten writes these from the prime while runs are in flight and commits them later through weft sync, so any Finalize that runs between a write and its sync commit hits the precondition.
Workaround today: `lyx fabric commit` in the prime, then `lyx loom resume` in the pair.
Expected: Finalize's merge precondition ignores, or commits first, the parent weft's own batten records, so a sibling run's status write never blocks a landing.

### Teardown clears an abandoned run's claim (from `abandoned-run-claim`)

With `board-lock-running`, a board entry whose status has the run form (`<state> · <producer>`) refuses every scope change.
A run that ends without landing (stopped, abandoned, its pair removed) leaves that status behind, so the entry stays locked until someone clears it by hand (seen in the PR-Gate review of PR #482).
Batten's teardown of a run that did not land clears the claim, or sets a non-run status, so the task becomes editable again.

### Friction-Reflect reads the parent weft (from `reflect-reads-parent-weft`)

Seen (publish-recovery, 2026-10-10): Finalize blocked on "worktree dirty" from the prime weft's batten records (#501), and Friction-Reflect dismissed it as a process signal because the task worktree was clean.
Friction-Reflect also reads the parent weft's status (`lyx fabric status` in the parent) when a halt names a dirty worktree, so it attributes the halt to the right tree.

entries.title: Bench the chair-and-advisors Discussion against the solo writer before switching it on
entries.brief: Same tasks through both producers, compare review rounds, findings, tokens and time; the operator watches a live run before it goes on
entries.body:
## Seen

`discussion-multi-llm` adds a second Discussion producer: a chair that writes, with advisors that study the code and answer its design questions live.
The default keeps the existing solo Discussion-Write, so landing it changes no run.

## Idea

Before any hub selects the chair-and-advisors producer, bench it against the solo writer on the same tasks: Discussion-Review rounds and findings, parent-review outcome, token cost per seat, and wall time.
Then the operator watches it in action on at least one live run before it is switched on.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-10)

- Models for the trial: the chair on `opus[medium]`, one advisor on `sonnet[high]`.
- Not in production until the bench and a watched run have shown it holds.

## Retiring the single producer (operator, 2026-10-10)

The seats producer with an empty `discussion_advisors` list covers the single writer's job: one chair prompt for every advisor count says "use your advisors if you have any; with none, decide each question yourself as you judge best", with no conditional rendering.
Once that is tested, the single producer is parked, since seats with N=0 covers it; the bench should include an N=0 run against solo to show they match.

entries.title: Discussion advisors: operator-named areas per advisor on top of the landed all-advisors default
entries.brief: Each discussion_advisors entry takes an optional area (a lens, as in review fans); without one the advisor answers every question
entries.body:
## Seen

The chair-and-advisors Discussion (`discussion-multi-llm`) sends every question batch to every advisor, by the operator's PR-Gate ruling on PR #504 (2026-10-10).
The first draft instead gave each advisor its own area of the design, which narrows each advisor's view but spreads the study.

## Idea

Support both, selected per hub in `loom.yaml` (for example `discussion_advisor_mode: all | areas`, default `all`), with the value passed to the chair stencil as a marker.
Decide after `discussion-multi-llm-bench`, which can compare the two modes on the same tasks.

## Operator-named areas

The operator also wants to choose which area each advisor studies (2026-10-10), rather than leaving the split to the chair.
One shape: each `discussion_advisors` entry carries a model-spec plus an optional area, for example `{model: sonnet[high], area: error-handling}`, and the area names a lens text the advisor stencil includes, the way Burler's review fans name lenses (`correctness`, `error-handling`, `test-gaps`).
An entry without an area answers every question; an entry with one still sees every batch but answers from its lens.
This could replace the `all | areas` switch: the per-entry area is the selection.

entries.title: Master's wait stops waiting on a still-running background shell at a turn end
entries.brief: A gate run still in a background shell is cut off at a turn end and the run still reports done
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #505](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/505).

## What happened

Master's wait counted a turn end while a background shell was still running: an integration `lyx gate test --tags integration` run over several packages, piped through `grep` and `tail`.
The shell was reported only by the transcript, so the wait stopped waiting on it after `background_shell_wait_min` (10 minutes).
That turn end finished the run because Master's output files existed, and lyx did not stop the shell.
Shuttle then removed Master's strand, which ended the session and the shell with it.
The run's final outcome was `done`.

## Why it is abnormal

The integration test run was still in progress when the run finished, so its result was never seen by Master or the loom.
A run can report `done` with a gate tier unfinished, and the shell is killed silently rather than waited for or stopped explicitly.

## What to do

Decide whether a still-running background shell should hold the turn end past `background_shell_wait_min` when it is a gate run.
At minimum, make lyx stop the shell explicitly and record in the run that its result was discarded, so the outcome is not read as "tests passed".

Task: discussion-multi-llm. Notes: webster-background-shell.md

## Overlap

The shell-wait fault itself (#496) is in the scope of the running task `webster-replan-state`; this note adds the gate-run case, where a cut-off gate tier leaves the run reading as `done`.
Close it when that run lands if its fix covers a running gate shell.


## From issue #509

Imported from [issue #509](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/509).

Webster's wait stopped waiting on a background shell at Master's turn end.
The shells were `lyx gate test --tags integration` runs, still running when the wait counted the turn end.
The wait counts the turn end after `background_shell_wait_min` (10 minutes) for a shell only the transcript reports, and at once for one the Stop payload reports when Master's output files exist.
lyx did not stop the shell; shuttle removed Master's strand on finishing, which killed the session and the shell with it.
The same note was written for two separate shells in one run, and the run ended `stuck`.
In a later run the outcome was `done`, so the integration gate result Master was waiting for was never observed either way.

This is abnormal: the run can finish, or be held for the parent, while a verification Master started is still in flight and is then killed unobserved.

What to do: when a shell is still running at a turn end, either keep waiting until it exits or a hard limit, or stop it explicitly and record that its result was discarded, so the outcome does not depend on whether the output files already exist.

Provenance: task `driver-context`; notes `webster-background-shell.md`, `webster-background-shell-2.md`.

entries.title: Webster Master fixes a verify failure itself instead of spawning the fixer fork
entries.brief: Master edited and committed a test fix itself; the run-exit audit blocked it as a parent-write
entries.body:
## Seen

In `driver-context` (2026-10-10), Webster's Publish verify failed twice and passed on attempt 3.
On that attempt Master, running `sonnet[medium]`, fixed the failing assertion itself (`Edit` on `internal/stencilcli/cli_integration_test.go`, then `git add` and `git commit`, 99d75755c), although its stencil sends verify failures to one fixer fork.
The fix was correct, but the run-exit audit flagged it as a parent-write and blocked the run, which then had to revert the file, `accept-audit` and redo the fix through a fork.

## Idea

Make the rule harder to skip: state it at the point Master reads a verify failure, not only in its rules list, or give Master a verb that spawns the verify fixer so the path of least resistance is the right one.
Check whether `sonnet[medium]` as Master skips such rules more often than a stronger model.

entries.title: Lens fan: master pre-reads the cited code before forking, forks get a read budget
entries.brief: Make the lens fan work as designed: the master reads the cited code (and judges nothing) before forking, each fork has a tool-call budget, and Discussion and Plan use their own fans
entries.body:
## Seen

The lens fan's design: the master reviewer reads most of what the round needs first, then forks, so each lens fork inherits that reading through the cache and needs little new reading, which keeps a fork cheap enough for a Sonnet medium reviewer.
The first fanned run (`webster-replan-state`, Discussion rounds 1-4 and Plan round 1) did not work that way; the analysis is in `fan-usage-report`:

- The master forked after reading only the target, instructions and stencil (39-74k context), no code, then told every fork to verify the Decisions' premises against the code.
  In Discussion round 1 the master read 19 code files first, and its forks took 32 turns and 152k fresh tokens; rounds 2-4 took 81-125 fork turns and 435-485k fresh.
- Inheritance through the cache works; cost scales with fork turns, about 3.5-4k fresh tokens per turn.
  32-46% of fork file reads duplicated another fork's.
- Fanned Discussion rounds cost 301-638k fresh against 86-121k for solo Opus rounds; Plan round 1 cost 901k fanned against 202-227k solo.
  The fan raised more MEDIUM and LOW findings, not more BLOCKING ones, and about half of raw fork findings were duplicates across lenses.

The responsible text is `clusterRulesBlock` in `internal/burlerengine/prompt.go`: "After exploring the target fully" never says to read the code the target cites, and "Fetch only what your lens needs" sets no budget.
The `standard` fan also points code lenses at design documents.

## Idea

Revise the fan so it works as designed:

- the master is told every lens of the fan up front, and before it spawns any fork it explores, for each lens, what that lens will need and reads it, so the forks inherit one shared reading instead of each exploring on its own (lyx cannot pick the relevant code itself: Discussion review is exploratory, so the master's judgment chooses what to read);
- the master judges nothing before the fork point: a review written before forking would colour every fork, so the master's own holistic review stays after the forks are spawned;
- each fork is told its context already holds the code, and gets a tool-call budget (about 6) for reading only what is missing; forks spending their budget show in the usage record that the master read too little;
- Discussion-Review and Plan-Review use the `discussion` and `plan` fans instead of `standard`.

Estimate: about 200-250k fresh tokens per round, about 2x a solo Opus round instead of 5-6x.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-10)

- The fan stays off in the hub until this task lands and a fanned run shows the estimate holds.
- Until then Discussion-Review and Plan-Review run solo on `opus[medium]`, and Webster-Review on `sonnet[medium]`.

entries.title: Plan format has no way to insert a card or remove a card file
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #508](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/508).

Plan cards are numbered contiguously and each card file name is tied to its number.
A Plan-Review fix that needed one new card ahead of card 8 therefore renumbered cards 8 to 19, twelve files.

The fixer rules allow file changes only through Edit or Write and name no way to rename or remove a file.
The fixer rewrote each card under its new name and removed the old files with `rm`, which the rules neither allow nor forbid.

This is abnormal: a routine plan edit forces a fixer to guess at an unstated rule and do a bulk, error-prone rewrite.

What to do, either of:
- add a plan verb that inserts a card and renumbers the rest;
- state a rule for removing a file inside the fixer's write surface.

Provenance: task `driver-context`; note `burler-plan-r1.md`.
